questions.question: In a Tornado-style mixer, what is the primary purpose of the Merkle root?
options: Commit to the set of deposit commitments so withdrawals can prove membership
Encrypt the recipient address so it can be revealed later
Generate randomness for the prover to build a witness
Store a list of nullifiers to prevent double spends
questions.explanation: The root is a compact commitment to all deposited commitments; a withdrawal proves its commitment is included in a tree with that root.

questions.question: What does a nullifier (via its public nullifier hash) prevent in a mixer?
options: Double spending the same note in two withdrawals
Reorgs from changing the Merkle root history
Front-running of deposits by copying calldata
Users from withdrawing too quickly after depositing
questions.explanation: A nullifier hash is a one-time tag derived from a note; once spent, the contract rejects any second spend of the same note.

questions.question: Which items must be public inputs to the verifier for a mixer withdrawal?
options: Merkle root, nullifier hash, and recipient/relayer/fee
Secret, nullifier, and Merkle path sibling hashes
Leaf index and Merkle path directions only
Deposit commitment preimage (secret || nullifier)
questions.explanation: The verifier checks a statement bound to public values: which root is claimed, which nullifier is being spent, and who gets paid (plus relayer/fee if supported).

questions.question: In a real ZK mixer, which data should remain private witness (not revealed on-chain)?
options: Leaf index and Merkle inclusion path (siblings/directions)
Merkle root and nullifier hash
Recipient and relayer addresses
Fee amount paid to the relayer
questions.explanation: ZK hides *which* deposit was spent by keeping the leaf index and path private while still proving membership against a public root.

questions.question: What breaks if the proof statement does NOT bind the recipient address?
options: A mempool observer can copy the proof and redirect funds (proof theft)
The Merkle tree can no longer be updated with new deposits
The nullifier hash stops preventing double spends
Withdrawals become linkable because the root becomes private
questions.explanation: If recipient isn’t part of the proven statement, an attacker can replay the same proof with a different recipient and steal the withdrawal.

questions.question: Why is a mixer deposit typically a fixed denomination (e.g., exactly 1 ETH) per pool?
options: So amounts don’t trivially link deposits to withdrawals by value
Because Merkle trees cannot store variable-length leaves
Because SNARK verifiers can only handle one amount value
So the nullifier hash has a consistent size
questions.explanation: If amounts vary, observers can match unique values or patterns; fixed denominations keep the anonymity set meaningful.

questions.question: Which of the following is an operational privacy leak even if the ZK proof is sound?
options: Withdrawing immediately after depositing with a unique gas-price pattern
Using domain-separated hashes for commitments
Checking nullifier hashes on-chain before accepting a withdrawal
Binding recipient/relayer/fee inside the proof statement
questions.explanation: Timing and transaction metadata can link actions in practice; cryptographic soundness does not guarantee privacy under chain analysis.

questions.question: A contract stores (1) deposit commitments and (2) spent nullifier hashes. What is the minimal additional thing it needs to verify withdrawals?
options: A way to validate a proof against an accepted Merkle root (a root registry or incremental tree)
A reversible encryption scheme for the commitment preimage
A per-user balance table for depositors
A trusted oracle that reveals which deposit index was used
questions.explanation: The verifier must know which roots are valid (either by maintaining the tree on-chain or accepting a set of recent roots) to check membership proofs.
